::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="FAQ: What are the differences between GitHub and GitLab?"}

[GitHub]({{< var links.github >}}) and [GitLab]({{< var links.gitlab >}}) are both **platforms for hosting Git repositories** and collaborating on projects.
They are not replacements for Git: Git is the version control system that runs on your computer, while GitHub and GitLab are remote hosting services that store Git repositories on the internet or on a server.
The Git commands in this book work in the same way with both platforms.

The two platforms share many features, including repositories, issues, pull requests or merge requests, code review, wikis, releases, and continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD).
Some differences are:

- **Terminology:** GitHub calls a proposed change a *pull request*, while GitLab calls it a *merge request*.
On GitHub, users and repositories can be organized in *organizations*. On GitLab, the equivalent is a *group*.
- **CI/CD:** GitHub uses [GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions), configured in `.github/workflows/`. GitLab uses [GitLab CI/CD](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/), configured in a `.gitlab-ci.yml` file.
- **Hosting:** GitHub is primarily used as a cloud service at [github.com]({{< var links.github >}}).
GitLab is also available as a cloud service at [gitlab.com]({{< var links.gitlab >}}), but its Community Edition can additionally be installed and operated on your own server.
This is why many universities and research institutions, including the University of Hamburg and the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, run their own GitLab instances.
- **Popularity and ecosystem:** GitHub is the largest platform for open-source projects and has a very large ecosystem of integrations.
GitLab is particularly common in organizations and research institutions that value self-hosting and an integrated DevOps platform.
- **Free plans:** Both platforms offer free plans, but the included features and limits differ and can change over time.
Check the current [GitHub pricing](https://github.com/pricing) and [GitLab pricing](https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/) pages before choosing a plan.

**Which one should you use?** In most cases, use the platform that your institution, your research group, or your collaborators use.
If you are free to choose, GitHub is a good default because of its popularity and large community, while GitLab is a strong choice if you need to host repositories on your own infrastructure.

:::
